extracted.intended_audience: educated readers and students of natural philosophy, biology, geology, astronomy, and sociology (general-scientific audience)
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length exposition of a proposed universal 'Law of Evolution' describing evolution as an integration of matter with concomitant dissipation of motion, and illustrating this law across astronomy, geology, biology, language, and society. The text distinguishes primary and secondary integrations and gives multiple examples supporting the law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolution defined as integration of Matter and dissipation of Motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Evolution is always fundamentally an integration of Matter and dissipation (loss) of Motion; every sensible existence reaches its concrete shape through processes of concentration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the primary, unifying statement to be used when judging phenomena as evolutionary: look for concentration (integration) of matter accompanied by loss or dissipation of motion. The claim is intended as a general law applying to aggregates of all orders (astronomical, geological, organic, social, linguistic, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between simple and compound Evolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple Evolution: evolution that is integrative only (primary aspect). Compound Evolution: evolution accompanied by secondary redistributions leading to further transformations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether an evolutionary case is merely the primary integration of matter or whether secondary re-distributions (local integrations, formation of parts, increased combination among parts) have accumulated. The rate of primary redistribution (rapid => simple; slow => allows secondary effects => compound) is diagnostic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rate of primary redistribution as determinant of aggregate complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary redistribution ends in forming aggregates which are simple where it is rapid, but which become compound in proportion as its slowness allows the effects of secondary re-distributions to accumulate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating an evolving system, consider the pace of the primary concentrating process: rapid concentration yields simple wholes; slower concentration permits layered, secondary changes producing compound structure (multiple parts, internal differentiation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary aspect focus for exposition (methodological guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is convenient to devote attention first to evolution under its primary aspect, tacitly recognizing secondary aspects only as necessary; the secondary redistributions can be treated in subsequent focused chapters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a methodological rubric for analysis/exposition: present the primary integrative changes first for clarity, then treat secondary integrations (each limited to a particular trait) in turn to avoid confusion from entangled transformations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local (secondary) integrations: formation of parts and increased combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Along with formation of a larger mass, there is drawing together and consolidation of matter into parts, and an increasingly intimate combination among those parts (e.g., embryonic organs forming, bones coalescing, tissues increasing in density).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and describe local consolidations (organs, strata, social subgroups) that accompany or follow primary integration; examples include heart forming from a pulsating vessel, liver cells consolidating into an organ, vertebrae coalescing, and increasing tissue density with age.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longitudinal integration (reduction and fusion of serial parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Longitudinal integration consists of the union or fusion of serial segments (e.g., reduction in number of segments in annelose animals, fusion of head and thorax in lobsters, fusion of vertebrae into sacrum or coccyx).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use longitudinal integration to diagnose progression from simple to more integrated forms: look for reduction in repetitive units and their fusion into consolidated regions (illustrated across embryos and across taxonomic ascents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transverse integration (coalescence across lateral elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transverse integration involves the union of lateral or paired structures into singular, median structures (e.g., double chains of ganglia uniting into a single chain; oviducts converging/coalescing into a single uterus in higher mammals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing development or evolution, note examples where paired/lateral elements become joined on the median line and form centralized structures; trace the degree of lateral coalescence across lower to higher forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrations among organisms (intraspecific and interspecific dependence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organisms become dependent on one another by gregarious tendencies (packs, sentinels, leaders), social insects with extreme consolidation, food-web dependencies (plants and animals, predators and prey), and specialized mutualisms (plants and particular insects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the degree of biological integration at the population/ecosystem level by examining behavioral cooperation, obligate sociality, trophic dependencies, and co-evolved mutualisms that make species dependent on each other within a habitat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Super-organic integrations (social, regulative, and operative consolidation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggregated organic bodies acting on one another produce phenomena not seen in single organisms — e.g., formation of tribes, states, regulative classes (governmental, military, ecclesiastical), operative industrial combinations (cities monopolizing industries), and the progressive consolidation of social groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For social evolution, distinguish internal unifications (establishment of regulative classes and castes) and operative/industrial integrations (urban agglomeration, monopolization of industries, specialized centers like exchanges and clearing-houses). Use historical and structural examples to show increasing stability and scale of integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Astronomical manifestations as evidence of the law
rubrics_metrics.description: Sidereal systems (clusters, nebulae) and the Solar System illustrate concentration of matter by gravitation and concomitant loss of motion (nebular hypothesis), with examples like condensation of nebulae, planets' internal condensation paralleling the whole, cometary retardation, and the Sun's radiated heat indicating loss of contained motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat astrophysical observations (nebulae stages, clusters, double stars, comet/planet retardation, solar radiation) as empirical instances of the integration/dissipation principle when arguing the law's applicability at cosmic scales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geological manifestations as evidence of the law
rubrics_metrics.description: Geologic history (Earth's cooling from molten state, formation of crust, superficial solidification, diminution of bulk by corrugation, development of continents and mountain systems, accumulation of extensive sedimentary strata) exemplifies concentration of matter concurrent with loss of contained motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use geological transitions (vapor condensation into oceans, crust thickening, mountain formation, large-scale sedimentation) as indicators of primary and secondary integrations in planetary evolution; relate local integrations (islands, continents) to increasing rigidity and crustal thickening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organic growth as integration by concentration of formerly diffused elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Plants and animals grow by concentrating elements previously diffused (gases or dispersed in other organisms); embryonic development especially shows absorption of nutriment and drawing-in to a germinal center, with organs consolidating out of surrounding tissues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In biological analysis, emphasize growth as a process of material concentration into organized structures: note early embryonic phases where growth is primarily absorption, and subsequent differentiation where parts consolidate and diverge to form organs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language evolution: agglutination, coalescence, and frequency-driven contraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Lower (uncivilized) languages show compounding (agglutination) with long polysyllabic words and separable elements; higher languages show progressive integration (reduction to dissyllables/monosyllables, fused vowels, inflectional contraction). Frequency of repetition accelerates coalescence (common words contract most).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using linguistic data as evidence of evolution, look for compounding vs fusion, historical phonological changes (e.g., Anglo-Saxon to English examples), loss of inflectional syllables, vowel fusion, and greater contraction in most-frequent terms as markers of integration.
